Reviewer 1 read the result as a weak pass by the letter of the strictly-dominant prong; reviewer 2 read it as failed (it wrote 'strictly dominant', which the critic did not). result.delta_one_sentence: B takes A's core mechanism (a linear probe on the answer-position residual stream, scored by within-question ranking AUC against majority voting, with a 0.60 line) to a single long-thinking math model, adds family and near-duplicate grouped splits, nested layer selection and a required gain over output-only confidence features including vote share, and uses the result only as a preregistered four-line gate for a later study, not as a predictive law across settings.
result.reasoning: Same mechanism: both run one teacher-forced pass per sampled answer, read the residual stream at the position that emits the answer token, fit a standardized L2 logistic correctness probe, use the mean within-question ranking AUC over mixed-correctness questions as the key quantity (both with a line near 0.60), and compare probe-driven aggregation with majority voting. The differences are in setting and rigor, not mechanism. B uses a thinking-mode reasoning model with long traces, reads after the reasoning ends, and does probe-weighted voting where A uses argmax selection. A is the stronger contribution. It reports results across fifteen model-benchmark settings and makes a falsifiable, actionable claim: medium-difficulty decodability predicts the gain of selection over voting, with r=0.96 in sample and 0.75 from calibration to deployment. It also gives a stylized model that explains where the boundary falls, why selection wins on hard questions whatever the decodability, and why voting gets worse there with more samples. That is a general diagnostic with mechanistic backing. B is a careful, compute-capped gate on one model. Its own design says passing licenses only a later factorial study, so it can yield at most a go/no-go, not a finding about the world. B does fix real weaknesses in A. First, A picks the operating layer by maximizing the pooled ranking metric on the same cross-validated data, a mild optimistic bias; B selects layer and regularization by nested family-grouped log loss. Second, A groups by question only, so near-duplicates and shared contest provenance can leak; B groups by family. Third, and most important, A never shows the probe beats cheap output-only signals such as token log-probabilities, entropy, length or vote share; B requires a positive paired increment over exactly those. B also notes that the middle-difficulty share cannot be identified from six draws and substitutes the contested-draw share, a subtle point that A's difficulty binning skips. Those are good controls for a follow-up or replication, but as a contribution B is a stricter, narrower pilot of A's idea, not a new mechanism or a broader result.

largest_defect: Feasibility and decisiveness: under its own registered caps the gate cannot reach the decision it exists for. On measured Qwen3-8B thinking-mode data (2609.32035, already cited as C03: Table 9 mean output tokens MATH-500 5,251, AMC 10,376, AIME 16,058; Table 13 accuracy 0.957/0.896/0.722; Table 8 danger zone 0.034/0.060/0.170), the 8.0 GPU-h cap rule (N >= 560 at 1.2 x the high projection), the S line (kappa6 >= 0.10) and I6 (at least 80 mixed held-out questions) cannot all hold. Workloads cheap enough to be admitted sit at about MATH-500 difficulty, where sharp LP bounds give kappa6 <= 0.063 and mixed6 <= 0.114 (at most about 45 mixed held-out questions), so STOP_SPREAD plus INCONCLUSIVE_N follow by construction; workloads contested enough to pass S (AMC or AIME level) are inadmissible under S2's own frontier (N_max about 326 and 165). The likely verdicts, INFEASIBLE or INCONCLUSIVE_N/STOP_SPREAD, read none of D, F or H, and both are predictable today with no GPU. Reviewer 1 (claude-opus-5-5, total 56) named this and reproduced the feasibility refuter's LP bounds with its own script; reviewer 2 (qwen3.6-35b-a3b, total 54, the authoritative score) named the identification defect instead (the registered answer position, the token before the first token inside the last \boxed{...}, moves with the answer's leading character under Qwen3's byte-level BPE, so a linear gate can learn a tokenizer artefact that the floor and I3/I4 cannot catch) and rated feasibility PARTLY_MEETS on the same cap-versus-workload argument. The recorder takes feasibility as the single largest defect because it is upstream: while it stands, D, F and H are never read, so repairing the identification defect alone yields no decision; the identification repair (a format-invariant position, answer-string and logit-gap/self-certainty floor features, F as the paired increment) is a cheap registration change, whereas feasibility needs a redesign or an owner admission under D24.

The cost cap and the decision lines want opposite workloads, and measured Qwen3-8B data leaves no workload where both hold. The gate cannot reach a decision under its own cap rule.

I took Qwen3-8B thinking-mode numbers from 2609.32035, which the proposal already cites as C03 (same T 0.6 / top-p 0.95 / top-k 20 sampling, same 32,768-token cap; Tables 8, 9, 13). Its AIME set (90 problems) and AMC set (83 problems) have the same sizes as the AI-MO validation sets behind stratum A6. I fed those numbers into the proposal's own S2 constants and its registered admission rule: 1.2 x the high projection, smoke 0.25 + P0 1.0, total caps at most 8.0, N between 560 and 800.

(1) MATH-500 level: mean 5,251 tokens, accuracy 0.957. The measured 0.55% truncation implies a length CV of about 1.17, which is outside S2's 0.6 to 0.9 grid. This is the only difficulty that clears the rule (N up to about 828). But the sharp upper bounds, taken over every pass-rate distribution consistent with the measured accuracy and danger-zone share (0.034), are mixed6 ≤ 0.114 and kappa6 ≤ 0.063. That gives at most about 45 mixed held-out questions in expectation at N = 800, against I6's minimum of 80, and kappa6 sits below the 0.10 line. So the outcome is INCONCLUSIVE_N plus STOP_SPREAD by construction. The proposal's own correction 4 already says the spread line "would likely fail by construction" at MATH-level traces.

(2) AMC level: 10,376 tokens, accuracy 0.896, kappa6 about 0.11 to 0.13. This is roughly the least difficulty at which S could pass. The caps allow N_max of about 326, below the 560 floor, so the result is INFEASIBLE. N = 560 would need 12.6 GPU-h of caps.

(3) AIME level: N_max is about 165, so again INFEASIBLE.

Mixed questions per GPU-second are linear in how questions are split across strata. So no mix of these difficulty levels gets past about 59 expected mixed held-out questions under the registered caps, whatever the N floor.

S1's decisiveness figures (D PASS 0.95 at AUC 0.70, about 117 mixed of 320) come from scenario S7: accuracy 0.687, mixed6 0.365, kappa6 0.174. That is AIME-like difficulty. At N = 640 it would need about 26.4 GPU-h of caps under S2's own constants, 3.3 times the admission line.

What happens in practice: the workload rule's eligibility test (tau_s ≥ 0.05 from 20 questions x 2 draws) screens out almost nothing, and the rule keeps the three cheapest strata. All six candidate strata are MATH Level 5, olympiad or AIME/AMC problems, at or above AMC difficulty, which is the only nearby measurement and already over the admissible mean. So the likely verdict is INFEASIBLE, far above the owner's 0.25 prior. In the unlikely case the rule admits something, the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE_N/STOP_SPREAD. Neither outcome reads D, F or H, which the proposal says are the point: does a learned selector justify the 30 to 40 GPU-h 2x2. Both outcomes can be predicted today without using any GPU.

Identification.strongest_argument:
The registered answer position changes with the answer's format, so D and F can be produced by a tokenizer artefact rather than by an internal correctness signal. No registered check can detect this, and the floor does not control for it.

(1) The position is defined as "the token immediately before the first token inside the last \boxed{...}" (proposal lines 326-332; registration design decision 15). Under Qwen3's byte-level BPE, the pre-tokenizer regex merges the opening brace with a non-digit first character into a single token: '{-', '{\\', '{x', '{n', '{(', '{$' all exist in the 151,643-token vocabulary. So '\boxed{12}' tokenizes as [boxed, '{', '1', '2', '}'] and the state is read at '{'. But '\boxed{-12}', '\boxed{\frac..}', '\boxed{x=3}', '\boxed{(2,3)}' and '\boxed{\infty}' tokenize as [boxed, '{-' or '{\\' or '{x' or '{(' ...], so the state is read one token earlier, at 'boxed'. (The alternative reading, that these draws have no answer position, instead removes them from D by answer format.) Two draws of the same question that differ only in sign, or in integer versus LaTeX form, are therefore read at different structural positions.

A linear gate fitted on training families learns "read at '{'" as a proxy for correct wherever wrong answers tend to differ in leading-character class from correct ones (sign errors, unsimplified or LaTeX forms on integer-answer AIME, AMC and MATH items). That proxy transfers across families. Two things fail to catch it:
- The floor (registration lines 232-236) has no answer-string features.
- I3 (within-question label permutation) and I4 (prompt-only probe, 0.5 by construction) pass with probability 0.997 to 1.0 even when the artefact is the only signal.

On S1's own generator, a gate whose only real within-question AUC is 0.55 has P(STOP_DECODE) 0.577 without the artefact. With it, P(STOP_DECODE) is 0.067 when 20% of wrong answers flip answer class, and P(PASS_D) is 0.42 at a 40% flip rate.

(2) F is a head-to-head gap (gate minus floor; registration lines 275-277), but STOP_REDUNDANT is read as "adds less than 0.02 within-question AUC over free output signals" (proposal line 600). Those are different estimands. On S1's generator, with gate AUC 0.66 and floor 0.70, STOP_REDUNDANT fires 44% of the time, while gate plus floor beats the floor by +0.046 (L90 above 0 in 62% of runs).

(3) Conditioning D on mixed questions picks out grader errors. Format-variant false negatives from math-verify that I1's 98% bar tolerates (draw-level error 0.6 to 1.2%) make 5.7 to 10.8% of D's population spuriously mixed and add 1.0 to 2.1 points to kappa6. That is inside S's indeterminate band (0.08 to 0.14).

(4) S1 never fits the gate (gate-sim.py lines 277-279 draw the scores directly from a known separation). In a toy model where the oracle within-question AUC is 0.70, the registered 4,096-feature fit on 320 training questions reads 0.51 to 0.57. So STOP_DECODE and STOP_REDUNDANT can be produced by training-set size and by the 4,096-versus-8 dimensionality gap, not by an absence of decodability.
Identification.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any of the following changes, registered before the freeze, would answer this lens. Without them the default stays refuted.

1. **A format-invariant answer position.** For example, always the 'boxed' token, or the last token before '\boxed'. Verify it with the Qwen3-8B tokenizer at revision b968826d against every answer form in the data manifest.
2. **An answer-string and lexical floor arm.** Leading-character class, integer-ness, magnitude, token count, whether the answer appears in the problem statement, hedging-word counts, and logit gap and self-certainty from the stored top-20 logprobs. D and F should also be decision-bearing after residualising on answer-type indicators.
3. **F redefined as the paired increment.** That is, the gate plus floor minus the floor, keeping gate minus floor as a reported number, and rewording STOP_REDUNDANT to match.
4. **An I1 audit that oversamples mixed held-out questions.** Adjudicate every answer class where the draws of a held-out question disagree, and recompute D and S on the adjudicated labels.
5. **S1 rerun with a real fitting step.** Fit a 4,096-feature gate on N/2 training questions, widen the C grid, and add a rule that STOP_DECODE cannot fire while the 25/50/75% learning curve is still rising.
6. **GO decided on one common population.** For example, a decision-bearing hard-bin selection-gain line, or D restricted to contested questions with completed wrong answers.
7. **Families as global connected components across strata.** Split by component, and fold split-seed variation into the intervals.

Alternatively, a pre-freeze CPU audit on stored thinking-model banks (for example the released Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking banks, C40) could show that under 3% of within-question correct/wrong pairs differ in their answer's leading-character class. Together with a mixed-question grader audit at 99% or better, that would neutralise the main threats empirically.

Novelty.strongest_argument:
The gate is CASE's protocol (arXiv 2608.17124) moved to a new model and task. Each of its four decision lines, and its leakage controls, already appears in a primary source. What is left is one unmeasured cell: Qwen3-8B in thinking mode with traces up to 32k tokens on competition math, with all four lines measured on one set of draws. That cell is a data point. It is not a novelty delta, and CASE itself names the extension as future work ("extending the readout ... to free-form generation"; "testing across ... task families", Sec. 8 Future directions).

(1) Line D (decodability in thinking mode) is already published for thinking models, and the proposal does not cite the closest source. PAIR (arXiv 2609.36461, v1 2026-09-29), Table 2, reports a "Pre-Ans token" probe: StandardScaler, PCA-128 and logistic regression on the state just before the answer. Its within-question AUC on held-out MATH-500 questions is 0.79 for Qwen3-4B with /think and 0.87 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, with Best-of-32 selection. Its Table 1 also shows the gap between across-question and within-question AUC, which is the leakage point the proposal relies on. Three of the cells' own counted queries returned PAIR (FR-12, FR-20, FR-45), but it was never read or cited. HSRM (2608.30841, Table 2) adds within-problem AUROC of 0.736 and 0.884 with answer-only extraction in thinking mode. The proposal's own prior for P1 is "likely pass".

(2) Line F (gain over an output-only floor) and the length-residualised control are CASE's own Sec. 6.8 and Supplementary S14: self-certainty, sequence log-probability and predictive entropy are scored on the same pools from the same forward pass, and a within-question length residualisation is included. HSRM Table 8 compares a hidden-state verifier with log-probability, entropy and length scorers on a disjoint split; the gains range from -1.6 to +2.4 points. An ICLR 2027 submission, Xpbbetf285 ("Can Correctness Readouts Choose the Right Answer? A Question-Level Audit of Compact KV-Cache Signals", 2026-09-18), audits pooled versus within-question ranking against hidden-state and likelihood controls. It finds that same-pool majority voting matches or beats the readouts. That is the gate's D/F/H design template with a different signal.

(3) Line H (harm against voting) is covered on the gate's own model. On Qwen3-8B in thinking mode, 2609.32035 finds weighted voting never beats majority voting, while TrajSelector (2510.16449) has a hidden-state selector that does. CASE's argmax-versus-voting rule and ARBITER (2605.26172: hidden-state evidence added on top of consensus, no net-negative cases) cover the weighted-vote form.

(4) Line S: the share of questions with mixed outcomes is an elementary statistic. The claim that the mixing distribution is not identified from k trials (presented as "synthesis adds an identification result") is classical binomial-mixture theory (Wood 1999, Ann. Stat., doi 10.1214/aos/1017939148, building on Lindsay).

(5) Family-grouped splits, nested layer and C selection by grouped log loss, and cluster-bootstrap intervals are standard practice that the proposal itself cites (Roberts 2016, Cawley and Talbot 2010, Obuchowski 1997).

The owner already rates the gate as "low as novelty (a transfer test)" and says "CASE is the stronger contribution". Measured against the published components, the gate is a recombination plus one model and workload cell. Under the default-to-refuted rule, novelty is refuted.

result.closest_prior_id: arXiv:2608.17124 (CASE: A decodability criterion predicts when hidden-state selection beats majority voting in large language models; Wang, Hong and Bagci; v1 2026-08-17)
result.closest_prior_mechanism_paragraph: Instruction-tuned language models of several sizes, general and domain-specialized, answer multiple-choice and short free-response questions, and several candidate answers are sampled per question with short outputs. For every candidate, one teacher-forced pass records the residual-stream activation at every layer at the position that produces the answer token. A standardized, L2-regularized logistic classifier of candidate correctness is fitted at a late layer, with all training and evaluation done in five-fold cross-validation grouped by question so that no question appears in both training and test folds; the operating layer is the one that maximizes the pooled within-question ranking metric. Decodability is defined as the mean over questions with both correct and incorrect candidates of the within-question ranking AUC of the classifier score, which is free of question-identity leakage by construction, whereas a probe evaluated with random splits looks accurate only through that leakage. For each question the candidate with the highest out-of-fold score is selected and its accuracy is compared with majority voting, by difficulty bin, with bootstrap intervals over questions. Across fifteen model-benchmark settings, decodability on medium-difficulty questions predicts the gain of selection over voting (correlation 0.96 in sample and 0.75 from a calibration set to deployment) with a decision boundary near an AUC of 0.60, and a stylized model derives that the boundary depends on how much voting beats a random pick of the pool, that selection gains on hard questions where sampled errors concentrate regardless of decodability, and that voting worsens with more samples there. The diagnostic is offered as an inexpensive criterion, measured on a small labelled set before deployment, for choosing hidden-state selection over majority voting.
